newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Bjerregaard to propose liability White Paper.
newsitem.headline: Bjerregaard to propose liability White Paper.

text.p: Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard is to propose a white paper on environmental liability in the wake of a Commission orientation debate on the issue, a spokesman said on Wednesday.

The planned white paper would lay out three options for an EU-level legal instrument, ranging from a directive for a general liability system, Community accession to the Council of Europe's Lugano Convention or a narrower directive on liability for environmental damage alone.
"The outcome of the discussion in the Commission was that a white paper is going to be issued on the basis of a proposal from Mrs Bjerregaard," Nikolaus van der Pas told a news conference.

"It's going to be a consultative document. During the discussions in the Commission it became clear that it is a very complicated decision. Member states are not all that enthusiastic and there are major reservations in industry," he said.
"Nevertheless, it's clear that something has to be done," he said, adding that Bjerregaard had given no target date for the planned adoption of the white paper.

The European Environment Bureau, which represents a series of European non-governmental environment organisations, said in a recent statement it supported Community the 1993 Lugano Convention as "a good basis for a common EU-system".

It urged that an EU directive based on this should include in addition a system for paying compensation for irrevocable environmental damage, that the burden of proof be on the polluter to prove innocence and that there be rights of access to law in such cases for the public and environmental groups.

Bjerregaard's preparatory communication for Wednesday's discussions said five states -- Finland, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands -- were signatories to the Lugano Convention on environmental liability. Austria, meanwhile, has drafted national laws braodly in line with the convention.

It said Germany, Britain, Denmark and France "are known to oppose the approach" mapped out in the Convention, the first three because it conflicts with their national regimes and the latter because of questions about Community competence to accede to the Convention. Britain has raised similar questions.
